blocks.intro: Where leaks start in McHenry has a lot to do with the water and the age of the house.

items.h3: Hard Water Wears Valves and Fittings
items.body: Scale stiffens valves and wears seals, so drips start at fixtures and shutoffs sooner.
In homes from the 1970s and 1980s, some copper lines develop pinhole leaks, especially near fittings.
On a private well, a pressure tank or pump that cycles with no water running often means a leak somewhere.
Some lake-area homes sit empty part of the year. A small leak can run for weeks before anyone notices.

items.q: How do I check for a leak if I'm on a well?
items.preview: Turn off all water and listen for the pump.
items.answer: Turn off every fixture and appliance. If the well pump or pressure tank keeps cycling, water is leaking somewhere. Call us and we'll find it.

items.q: Can you find a leak under a concrete slab?
items.preview: Yes, with listening and tracing equipment.
items.answer: Yes. We use listening and tracing equipment to locate leaks under slabs, so we break only the concrete we need to.

items.q: Why is my shower leaking into the ceiling?
items.preview: A valve, drain or connection behind the wall.
items.answer: Usually a leaking valve, a loose connection or a failed drain seal. We find the exact source and fix it.

items.q: Is a small drip worth fixing?
items.preview: Yes. Small leaks cause mold and rot over time.
items.answer: Yes. A slow leak can cause mold and rot long before you see it. Fixing it early is cheaper.

items.q: How much does leak repair cost in McHenry?
items.preview: It depends on the leak and access. You get a flat price first.
items.answer: It depends on where the leak is, the pipe and how we reach it. We give you a flat-rate price before any work begins.
